title: Ja'far al-Sadiq's school
hook: the Ja'fari school, followed by Twelver Shia, is named for the sixth Imam
carry: the school of the sixth imam

segments.voice: Yesterday, where it's followed: the Hanbali lands, and your line: the smallest, the steadfast. What small thing did you see keep its shape? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

Sahih Muslim holds a long report of the Prophet's pilgrimage, told step by step, from setting out to the standing at Arafat. Look at who passed it on. Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from the Companion Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. Sunni hadith scholars carried that report through him, and call him al-Sadiq, the truthful. For Twelver Shia Muslims he is also Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam. One man, honored on both sides. Today, the school of law that carries his name.
screen: `A PILGRIMAGE REPORT IN SAHIH MUSLIM.` → `TOLD THROUGH JA'FAR.` → `ONE MAN, HONORED ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: The Ja'fari school is the school of law followed by Twelver Shia Muslims. Twelvers recognize a line of Imams from the Prophet's family, beginning with 'Ali, and Ja'far is the sixth. He lived and taught in Medina, after his father, Muhammad al-Baqir. Shia tradition holds that the Imams carry the Prophet's knowledge, passed from one to the next, and that Ja'far taught openly, on law, on the Qur'an, on belief. That's why the school bears his name. Sunni Muslims honor him too, as a scholar of the Prophet's household. Reports say that Abu Hanifa and Malik, both met this month, sat with him or learned from him; scholars weigh those reports differently. So what does the school look like from inside? Its sources are the Qur'an and the sunnah. For Twelvers, the sunnah includes the teachings of the Imams, received through Shia collections such as al-Kafi, gathered by al-Kulayni. It uses reason, 'aql, which this block met a few weeks ago. And its jurists don't use analogy, qiyas, the way the Sunni schools do. In Shia reports, Ja'far himself warns against it. Here is one saying attributed to him in al-Kafi, paraphrased. Don't judge a man by how long he bows and prostrates; that may be a habit he'd feel lost without. Look instead at his truthfulness when he speaks, and at how he returns what was entrusted to him. It's a test for a person that skips the visible piety and goes straight to two plain things: the word you give, and the thing you were trusted with.
screen: `THE SCHOOL OF THE TWELVER SHIA.` · `HONORED BY SUNNI SCHOLARS TOO.` · `QUR'AN, SUNNAH, IMAMS, REASON.` · `TRUTHFUL SPEECH, A TRUST RETURNED.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one saying of his. Take the one from today. In your own words: don't judge by the length of the bowing; look at truthful speech and a trust returned. Say it once. Then think of someone you trust. Ask what earned it. Something they showed you, or something they kept? Then turn it around, gently. Is there a word you gave, or something you were lent, that's still waiting? Don't fix it yet. Just see it, and breathe. If you pray, you can ask to be trustworthy. The bell holds the time.
Ja'far al-Sadiq's school. The Ja'fari school of law, followed by Twelver Shia, named for the sixth Imam, Ja'far, called the truthful. Today's word.
Your line: the school of the sixth imam. Today, keep one small trust exactly: return the thing you borrowed, or do the thing you said you'd do. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.
